title: Πῆραι δύο
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 303 (= Perry 266). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Προμηθεὺς πλάσας ποτὲ ἀνθρώπους δύο πήρας ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀπεκρέμασε, τὴν μὲν ἀλλοτρίων κακῶν, τὴν δὲ ἰδίων, καὶ τὴν μὲν τῶν ὀθνείων ἔμπροσθεν ἔταξε, τὴν δὲ ἑτέραν ὄπισθεν ἀπήρτησεν.
sentences.tr: Promētheus plasas pote anthrōpous dyo pēras ex autōn apekremase, tēn men allotriōn kakōn, tēn de idiōn, kai tēn men tōn othneiōn emprosthen etaxe, tēn de heteran opisthen apērtēsen.
sentences.l: Prometheus, having once moulded men, hung two wallets from them, the one of other men's faults, the other of their own; and the one of the alien faults he set in front, but the other he hung behind.
sentences.i: When Prometheus had moulded men, he hung two wallets on them, one holding other men's faults and one holding their own; and the wallet of other men's he set in front, while the other he fastened behind.
sentences.n: Prometheus is the maker of mankind, and πλάσσω is the word for working clay — men are moulded like pots. κακά is 'bad things', here the failings a man carries about with him. ἀλλότρια and ὀθνεῖα both mean 'belonging to others', varied only for the ear. A πήρα is the leather wallet a traveller or shepherd slung on him, so both loads are worn, not carried in the hand.

sentences.t: Ἐξ οὗ δὴ συνέβη τοὺς ἀνθρώπους τὰ μὲν ἀλλότρια κακὰ ἐξ ἀπόπτου κατοπτάζεσθαι, τὰ δὲ ἴδια μὴ προορᾶσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ex hou dē synebē tous anthrōpous ta men allotria kaka ex apoptou katoptazesthai, ta de idia mē proorasthai.
sentences.l: From which indeed it came about that men look upon other men's faults from far off, but do not see their own before them.
sentences.i: And that is how it came about that men can make out other men's faults from a distance, and never see their own in front of them.
sentences.n: ἐξ ἀπόπτου is 'from a place with a clear view', and so from a long way off. προοράω is to see a thing in front of one, or beforehand — the two senses are one here, since what is behind you can be neither seen nor guarded against, and the name Προμηθεύς means 'forethinker'.

sentences.t: Τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ χρήσαιτο ἄν τις πρὸς ἄνδρα πολυπράγμονα, ὃς ἐν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ πράγμασι τυφλώττων τῶν μηδὲν προσηκόντων κήδεται.
sentences.tr: Toutōi tōi logōi chrēsaito an tis pros andra polypragmona, hos en tois heautou pragmasi typhlōttōn tōn mēden prosēkontōn kēdetai.
sentences.l: This story someone might use against a meddlesome man, who, being blind in his own affairs, cares for the things that belong to him in nothing.
sentences.i: One might use this story against a busybody, who is blind in his own affairs and takes trouble over matters that are no concern of his.
sentences.n: πολυπράγμων is the man busy about many things, and so the meddler; the word is always a reproach. κήδομαι takes the genitive of what one cares for. τὰ μηδὲν προσήκοντα, 'the things that belong to one in nothing', is a standing phrase of the collection (fables 150, 193, 281, and again at 304).
